title: Hariharaputra: son of Shiva and Vishnu
hookLine: a childless king out hunting hears a baby crying by the river, a small bell at its neck
carry: Hari and Hara are not rivals
tomorrow: a queen falls ill, and only tiger's milk will cure her. who goes?

cards: A crying sound, thin and high, somewhere near the river. The king of Pandalam is out hunting in the forest, and he stops his horse to listen. It isn't a bird.
He follows the sound down to the bank of the Pampa, and there, alone on the ground, is a baby boy, bright as a lamp, with a small bell tied around his neck. No mother. No hut.
No one. And the king has no children of his own.

teach.b: In the story as it's told in Kerala, a demoness named Mahishi has won a boon that makes her almost impossible to defeat.
Only a son born of Shiva and Vishnu together could overcome her, which sounds like a riddle with no answer. Here's the answer.
Vishnu once took the form of Mohini, an enchanting woman, and from Shiva and Mohini a child is born.

teach.h: HARIHARAPUTRA: SON OF HARI AND HARA
teach.b: So Ayyappa is called Hariharaputra, the son of Hari and Hara: Hari is a name of Vishnu, Hara a name of Shiva. That matters.
Hindus have long had Shaivas, devoted above all to Shiva, and Vaishnavas, devoted above all to Vishnu, and at times the two argued hard. The tradition keeps answering back.

Old temples carve Harihara, one figure, half Shiva and half Vishnu, as in the caves at Badami, and many teachers say Hari and Hara are one. Ayyappa makes it a family: one child with both of them as parents.
The baby is left by the river Pampa with a bell at his neck. The childless king of Pandalam finds him and longs to keep him.
In the telling, a holy man tells the king: raise him as your son, and the truth will come out in time.
So they call him Manikandan, which the story explains as the one with the bell at his throat.
The son of two gods grows up as an adopted prince, loved by a father who doesn't yet know who he is.

how: Devotees of Ayyappa tell how he was born of Shiva and Vishnu as Mohini, found as a baby by the Pampa river and raised by the king of Pandalam, and the Pandalam royal family keeps a special place in his worship.

games.q: what does “kerala's onam and ayyappa” mean?
o: a king welcomed home, and a god born of Shiva and Vishnu
a king sent away, and a god born to the Pandalam queen
a king crowned again, and a god born to a fisherman

games.q: the foundling by the river — tap the pairs.
p: Vishnu's form as an enchanting woman
the one with the bell at his throat

s: Ayyappa is told as the son of Shiva alone
he's Hariharaputra: born of Shiva and of Vishnu in the form of Mohini.
the king of Pandalam had no children when he found the baby
in the story, the childless king finds him by the river and raises him as his son.
old Hindu temples carve Harihara, a single figure half Shiva and half Vishnu
Harihara images, like the one in the caves at Badami, show the two gods in one body.

games.q: at a family dinner, an uncle devoted to Shiva and an aunt devoted to Vishnu start arguing whose god is greater. by Ayyappa's story, what fits?
o: point to Hariharaputra: in Ayyappa, Hari and Hara meet, and many Hindus honor both.
pick a side: every Hindu has to choose one god.
say Ayyappa proves Shiva wins, since Vishnu only took a borrowed form.
games.why: Ayyappa is the son of Hari and Hara, and Harihara images carve the two as one: in this tradition they aren't rivals.

practice: Let the breath settle. If you pray, say silently on the in-breath, Om Namah Shivaya, and on the out-breath, Om Namo Narayanaya: two names Hindu homes chant, sometimes in separate homes, meeting here in one breath.
If you don't pray, let the in-breath and the out-breath be two halves of one circle, and rest where they join.

wordCard.voice: Kerala's Onam and Ayyappa. Today, Ayyappa's beginning: the son of Hari and Hara, found as a baby by the Pampa river with a bell at his neck, and raised by the king of Pandalam. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: Hariharaputra, 'son of Hari and Hara', a name of Ayyappa as the son of Vishnu and Shiva.

carryVoice: Your line: Hari and Hara are not rivals. Their son was found by a river with a bell at his neck. That's today, done.
